sections.b: Teachers from Judea told the believers at Antioch that Gentiles could not be saved without circumcision (Acts 15:1), and believing Pharisees in Jerusalem said the same (Acts 15:5). Luke tells of three testimonies. Peter recalled how God gave the Spirit to Cornelius' household, made no distinction and cleansed their hearts by faith; to lay the law's yoke on them would be testing God, since Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus (Acts 15:7–11). Barnabas and Paul told of signs and wonders among the Gentiles (Acts 15:12). James, the Lord's brother, quoted Amos 9:11–12 in its Greek form, that the rebuilt house of David would lead the rest of humankind and the nations called by God's name to seek the Lord, and gave his ruling (Acts 15:13–21).

sections.h: The decree and its four rules
sections.b: The letter sent to Antioch, Syria and Cilicia lays "no heavier load" on Gentile believers than four things: food sacrificed to idols, blood, what is strangled and sexual sin (Acts 15:28–29). The most common view links them to the Torah's laws for the foreigner living in Israel (Leviticus 17:7–18:26), in the same order. Others see rules for shared meals, or compare the later rabbinic commandments for the descendants of Noah. The Western text, in Codex Bezae, drops "strangled" and adds the Golden Rule, turning food laws into moral laws (see the variants on Acts 15:20 and Acts 15:29). The decision is framed in the language of a city decree: "the Holy Spirit has decided, and so have we" (Acts 15:28).
sections.refs: Acts 15:19–29; Leviticus 17:7–15; Leviticus 18:6–26; Genesis 9:4; Acts 16:4; Acts 21:25

sections.b: Paul describes a private meeting in Jerusalem at which James, Peter and John recognized his mission to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:1–10). Most critical scholars and many others identify it with Acts 15. Others, among them Ramsay, F. F. Bruce, Richard Longenecker and Ben Witherington, identify it with the famine visit of Acts 11:29–30, which would put Galatians before the council and explain Paul's silence about the decree. A third group thinks Luke combined two meetings. The choice affects the dating of Galatians and how far Acts and Paul's letters agree.

common: The council decided that Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised to be saved.
James, the brother of Jesus, gave the deciding ruling.
uncommon: Some scholars think the decree was issued later, without Paul, and that Luke joined it to the council (compare Acts 21:25, where James tells Paul of it as if it were news).
A few think Galatians 2 and Acts 15 describe different meetings, with Galatians written before the council.

claude.title: Three witnesses
claude.body: The council hears three kinds of testimony, Peter's experience of the Spirit, Barnabas and Paul's signs, and James' Scripture, before a verdict is given. I suspect Luke shaped the scene on the Torah's rule that a matter stands on two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), so that Jewish-Christian readers would see the decision as lawful. This is my guess; Luke does not say it.

sections.h: Must Gentile believers be circumcised? Acts 15–16
sections.b: The question that divided the early church came to a head at Antioch, when teachers from Judea said, "If you are not circumcised as Moses' custom requires, you cannot be saved" (Acts 15:1). The Jerusalem council decided that Gentile believers need not be circumcised (Acts 15:19, 28). Immediately afterward Paul circumcised Timothy, whose mother was Jewish and father Greek, "on account of the Jews living in that area" (Acts 16:3). Readers have long asked how this fits Paul's refusal to circumcise Titus (Galatians 2:3) and his warnings in Galatians 5:2–6. The common answer is that Paul rejected circumcision as a condition of salvation for Gentiles, not as a Jewish practice; critics see Luke's portrait of a law-keeping Paul.
sections.refs: Acts 15:1–29; Acts 16:1–3; Galatians 2:3–5; Galatians 5:2–6; 1 Corinthians 7:18–19; Acts 21:21

sections.h: The law and Gentile believers in Acts 15
sections.b: Believing Pharisees argued that Gentile converts must be told "to keep the law of Moses" (Acts 15:5). Peter called it a yoke "that neither our ancestors nor we ourselves had the strength to carry" (Acts 15:10), a line that has been read as a complaint about the law and, by others, as a refusal to impose it on Gentiles. In Jewish teaching the yoke of the commandments was a joy (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). James' ruling kept four requirements drawn from the Torah's laws for foreigners (Leviticus 17–18), and added that Moses is read in every synagogue each Sabbath (Acts 15:21). The council did not tell Jewish believers to stop keeping the law (compare Acts 21:20–26).
sections.refs: Acts 15:5; Acts 15:10; Acts 15:19–21; Leviticus 17:8–15; Matthew 11:29–30; Acts 21:20–26

sections.h: Gentiles as Gentiles: the council and the God-worshipers
sections.b: Acts 15 settles that Gentiles who believe in Israel's Messiah belong to God's people without becoming Jews. James calls them "a people for his name" taken from the nations (Acts 15:14), using the word that normally means Israel, and reads Amos 9:12 of "all the nations over whom my name has been called" (Acts 15:17). The rules laid on them echo the laws for the foreigner living among Israel (Leviticus 17:8–15). In the cities of Paul's mission the first hearers were often Gentile "worshipers of God" who attended the synagogue, like Lydia (Acts 16:14) and the Greeks at Thessalonica (Acts 17:4) and Athens (Acts 17:17); an inscription from Aphrodisias shows such sympathizers listed beside Jews.
sections.refs: Acts 15:14–17; Acts 15:28–29; Leviticus 17:8–15; Acts 16:14; Acts 17:4; Acts 17:17; Acts 10:2

sections.b: The Jerusalem decree asked Gentile believers to keep away from food sacrificed to idols, from blood and from the meat of strangled animals (Acts 15:20, 29), rules that made shared meals with Jewish believers possible. Paul later discussed idol food without citing the decree (1 Corinthians 8–10), but the second-century churches kept away from blood: the martyrs of Lyons in AD 177 protested that Christians would not eat even the blood of animals. Churches today differ on whether the decree still binds (see the "Where Christians differ" card at Acts 15).
sections.refs: Acts 15:20; Acts 15:29; Acts 21:25; 1 Corinthians 8:1–13; 1 Corinthians 10:25–31; Revelation 2:14

sections.b: Two of the decree's four rules concern blood: Gentile believers are to keep away from blood and from what is strangled, meat not drained of its blood (Acts 15:20, 29). Both go back to the command to Noah, "Only, flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat" (Genesis 9:4), and to the laws binding Israelites and the foreigners living among them (Leviticus 17:10–14). The Western text drops "strangled" and so lets "blood" mean bloodshed, murder. The Orthodox canons still forbid eating blood; Jehovah's Witnesses apply the verse to blood transfusions; most other churches treat the rule as a temporary measure for peace between Jewish and Gentile believers.

The Jerusalem decree lists porneia, sexual sin, among the four things Gentile believers must avoid (Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25). Set beside rules drawn from Leviticus 17, it may refer above all to the forbidden unions of Leviticus 18, such as marriage to close relatives, which bound Israelites and foreigners alike; or it may carry its broad sense. Revelation pairs it with idol food in the same way (Revelation 2:14, 20).
sections.refs: Acts 15:20; Acts 15:29; Acts 21:25; Leviticus 18:6–26; Revelation 2:14; Revelation 2:20

sections.h: The first council: Scripture, Spirit and church
sections.b: Acts 15 shows the church settling a dispute by gathering its leaders, hearing testimony, reading Scripture (Amos 9:11–12) and agreeing a decision announced with the words "the Holy Spirit has decided, and so have we" (Acts 15:28). Catholic and Orthodox teaching sees in it the pattern of the ecumenical councils; Reformed churches find in it the model for synods that judge by Scripture; Baptist and Congregational churches stress that it was counsel freely received. The Bereans, who checked Paul's preaching against the Scriptures every day (Acts 17:11), are also often cited in the debate over Scripture and tradition.

At Philippi two whole households were baptized: Lydia's, after the Lord opened her heart (Acts 16:14–15), and the jailer's, in the middle of the night, after Paul and Silas told the word of the Lord "to him and to everyone in his house" (Acts 16:32–33). Acts tells of similar household conversions with Cornelius (Acts 10:44–48; 11:14) and Crispus (Acts 18:8), and Paul baptized the household of Stephanas (1 Corinthians 1:16). Whether these households included infants is a classic point of disagreement between churches that baptize infants and those that baptize believers only.
sections.refs: Acts 16:14–15; Acts 16:30–34; Acts 10:44–48; Acts 11:14; Acts 18:8; 1 Corinthians 1:16

sections.b: In Acts the Spirit directs the church's decisions and journeys. The council's letter says "the Holy Spirit has decided, and so have we" (Acts 15:28). Peter argues that God gave Gentiles the Spirit "as he had given him to us" (Acts 15:8). On the second journey the Holy Spirit stops Paul from speaking in Asia, and "the Spirit of Jesus," a phrase found nowhere else in the New Testament, blocks the way to Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7), before a vision calls them to Macedonia.

sections.h: The slave girl with a Python spirit
sections.b: At Philippi a slave girl "had a Python spirit," named for the serpent of Apollo's oracle at Delphi, and earned money for her owners by fortune-telling (Acts 16:16). Plutarch says such mediums were called pythōnes, and the Greek Old Testament uses a related word for the medium at Endor (1 Samuel 28:7). Her cry that Paul's party were "slaves of the Most High God" was true but unwelcome, and Paul drove the spirit out in Jesus' name (Acts 16:17–18). As at Ephesus, the gospel cost the trade in spiritual powers its profits (Acts 16:19; 19:19, 23–27).
sections.refs: Acts 16:16–19; 1 Samuel 28:7; Leviticus 19:31; Acts 8:9–24; Acts 13:6–12; Acts 19:13–19

sections.h: A slave girl and her owners
sections.b: The slave girl at Philippi had several owners who made money from her (Acts 16:16, 19). Once Paul freed her from the spirit, her owners' only concern was their lost income, and Luke does not say what became of her. The spirit itself called the missionaries "slaves of the Most High God" (Acts 16:17), the same word, doulos, that Paul and others used of themselves as servants of Christ.

Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with veterans, governed by two magistrates with lictors, proud of being Roman (Acts 16:12, 20–22, 35). Paul and Silas were charged with teaching customs unlawful for Romans, beaten with rods and jailed without trial. The next day Paul announced that they were Roman citizens, whose flogging without trial broke Roman law, and the frightened magistrates came to release them in person (Acts 16:37–39). At Thessalonica the charge was defying "Caesar's decrees" by proclaiming another king (Acts 17:7). Paul's citizenship protects him again in Jerusalem (Acts 22:25–29) and leads to his appeal to Caesar (Acts 25:11).

At Thessalonica the believers were accused of acting against "Caesar's decrees, by saying that Jesus is another king" (Acts 17:7). The charge echoes the one brought against Jesus before Pilate (Luke 23:2; John 19:12). E. A. Judge has suggested that the decrees were imperial bans on predicting a change of ruler. Paul's letters to Thessalonica speak of the Lord's "coming" (parousia), a word also used for an emperor's state visit, and warn against those who say "peace and security," close to the slogans of Roman rule (1 Thessalonians 4:15; 5:3).

sections.h: Paul in a city full of idols
sections.b: In Athens Paul's spirit was stirred to anger at a city "smothered in idols" (Acts 17:16). Yet his speech at the Areopagus argues gently: the Creator does not live in shrines made by hands or need human service, and since we are his offspring, God cannot be like gold or silver or stone (Acts 17:24–29). The argument follows Isaiah's mockery of idols (Isaiah 40:18–20; 44:9–20) and the Jewish case against images in the Wisdom of Solomon (13–15), put into terms Greek philosophers could accept. The Jerusalem decree had already asked Gentile believers to keep away from "the pollution of idols" (Acts 15:20).
sections.refs: Acts 17:16; Acts 17:22–29; Acts 15:20; Acts 15:29; Isaiah 40:18–20; Isaiah 44:9–20; Romans 1:22–23

sections.h: The one God preached to Athens
sections.b: Paul's Areopagus speech presents the God of Israel to Greek philosophers without quoting Scripture: the one who made the world and everything in it, Lord of heaven and earth, who needs nothing, gives life and breath to all, made every nation from one, and will judge the world through a man he raised from the dead (Acts 17:24–31). Its starting point is the altar "To an unknown god" (Acts 17:23): the God the Athenians sensed but did not know.

sections.h: "So that they would look for God"
sections.b: At the Areopagus Paul says that God arranged the times and places of the nations "so that they would look for God, in the hope that they might grope for him and find him. Yet he is never far off from a single one of us" (Acts 17:27). The verb for groping is used of the blind feeling their way (Deuteronomy 28:29; Isaiah 59:10). The verse joins the Old Testament call to seek the LORD (Deuteronomy 4:29; Isaiah 55:6) with a Greek sense of the divine as near to all. It has become a key text in debates about what people can know of God without Scripture (see the "Where Christians differ" card at Acts 17).
sections.refs: Acts 17:26–28; Acts 17:23; Deuteronomy 4:29; Deuteronomy 28:29; Isaiah 55:6; Isaiah 59:10; Romans 1:19–21

sections.b: Paul quotes the Greek poet Aratus: "For we are his offspring too" (Acts 17:28). He draws a biblical conclusion from it: if human beings, living persons, are God's offspring, God cannot be pictured in gold, silver or stone (Acts 17:29). The idea stands close to Genesis 1:26–27, where humans, not statues, are God's image, and to Luke's genealogy, which ends with "Adam, son of God" (Luke 3:38).

Paul tells the Athenians, who prided themselves on springing from their own soil, that God made every nation of humankind "from one person" and fixed their seasons and the limits of the places where they would live (Acts 17:26). The thought follows Genesis 10, where the nations spread out from Noah's family (Genesis 10:32), and the Song of Moses, where the Most High marks out the peoples' borders (Deuteronomy 32:8). The KJV's "of one blood" became a watchword against racism in America.

Paul's message in Athens was "Jesus and the resurrection," and some hearers thought he was announcing two foreign deities (Acts 17:18). His speech ends with God raising the appointed man from the dead as a guarantee of the coming judgment (Acts 17:31). At the words "resurrection of the dead" some sneered (Acts 17:32): Greeks could imagine an immortal soul, but not a raised body, and Aeschylus had made a god say at the founding of the Areopagus court that for the dead there is no rising. In Thessalonica Paul had argued from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise (Acts 17:3).

In Athens Paul debated with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, who called him a "seed-picker" and brought him to the Areopagus (Acts 17:18–19). His speech uses their language: to theion, "the Divine," the God who needs nothing, the unity of humankind, a line of Greek poetry (Acts 17:24–29). Luke adds a wry note on the Athenians' love of the newest thing (Acts 17:21). The scene is the New Testament's clearest meeting between the gospel and Greek philosophy.

In the synagogue at Thessalonica Paul argued from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that Jesus was the Messiah (Acts 17:2–3), the same case the risen Jesus made to his disciples (Luke 24:26, 46). Most Jews of the time expected a royal deliverer, not a crucified one, and Jewish readers have generally read passages such as Isaiah 53 of Israel. The accusers at Thessalonica turned the claim into a political one: "Jesus is another king" (Acts 17:7).

Acts says that "the Jews" in Thessalonica, moved by jealousy, raised a mob against Paul (Acts 17:5) and followed him to Berea (Acts 17:13). In context these are the synagogue members who rejected his message: some Jews in Thessalonica believed (Acts 17:4), and the Jews of Berea are praised as nobler for testing his preaching by the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). Paul's own sharpest words about Jewish opponents come in his letter to this church (1 Thessalonians 2:14–16). Read without this context, such passages were later used against Jews as a people.

At the council James, the Lord's brother, speaks last and gives the ruling that frees Gentile believers from circumcision while asking them to keep four rules drawn from the Torah (Acts 15:13–21). His use of the old Hebrew name "Simeon" for Peter (Acts 15:14) and his appeal to Moses read in every synagogue (Acts 15:21) fit the picture of James as a leader devoted to the law. The letter's opening, "greetings," is the same as in the letter of James (James 1:1).
sections.refs: Acts 15:13–21; Acts 12:17; Acts 21:18–25; Galatians 1:19; Galatians 2:9; Galatians 2:12; James 1:1

sections.b: Peter's speech at the Jerusalem council is his last appearance in Acts (Acts 15:7–11). He recalls how God chose him to bring the good news to Cornelius, gave the Gentiles the Spirit and cleansed their hearts by faith, and concludes that Jews are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus "the same way they are." After this Luke's story follows Paul.

At the Jerusalem council James quotes Amos' promise that God will "build again the fallen tent of David" (Acts 15:16; Amos 9:11) and reads it as fulfilled: with the risen Son of David, God's people are being restored, and the nations are coming to seek the Lord. The Dead Sea Scrolls also applied Amos 9:11 to the end times, the Florilegium (4Q174) to the Branch of David and the Damascus Document to the books of the law.

sections.h: The laws of Noah and the apostolic decree
sections.b: The rabbis later taught that all descendants of Noah are bound by seven commandments, among them bans on idolatry, sexual immorality, bloodshed and eating flesh torn from a living animal (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 56a–b). Readers have often compared them with the Jerusalem decree for Gentile believers, which forbids idol food, sexual sin, blood and strangled meat (Acts 15:20, 29). The comparison is suggestive, but the Noah laws are written down only later, and the decree follows the order of Leviticus 17–18 more closely. Both answer the same question: what does God ask of Gentiles who are not Jews?

At Troas Paul sees a vision in the night: a Macedonian man stands and begs him, "Cross over to Macedonia and help us!" (Acts 16:9). In Acts such night visions guide Paul at turning points (Acts 18:9–10; 23:11; 27:23–24), as dreams guided Joseph and the Magi in Matthew.

Hospitality carries the mission in Acts 16–17. Lydia urges Paul's party, "come into my home and stay" (Acts 16:15), and her house becomes the church's meeting place (Acts 16:40). The jailer brings Paul and Silas into his home and lays a table for them in the night (Acts 16:34). At Thessalonica Jason takes them in as guests and pays for it with a bond (Acts 17:7, 9).

Beaten and locked in the stocks at Philippi, Paul and Silas prayed and sang God's praises at midnight while the other prisoners listened (Acts 16:25), as the psalmist rises in the middle of the night to give thanks (Psalm 119:62). Tertullian later told imprisoned Christians that the leg feels nothing in the stocks when the mind is in heaven.

When an earthquake threw open the prison doors at Philippi, the jailer drew his sword to kill himself, believing the prisoners had escaped and he would answer for them with his life (Acts 16:27; compare Acts 12:19). Paul shouted, "Do yourself no harm!" (Acts 16:28), and the night ended with the jailer's baptism. It is the one story in the Bible where a suicide is prevented.

At Troas, after Paul's vision of the man of Macedonia, the narrative suddenly shifts to the first person: "we looked for a way to set out for Macedonia" (Acts 16:10). The "we" continues to Philippi (Acts 16:10–17) and returns later (Acts 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16). Tradition takes it as the author's own presence; others see a diary source, a literary convention of sea voyages, or a claim to authority.

sections.h: The council and the second journey (Acts 15–17)
sections.b: Paul and Barnabas argued against the teachers who demanded circumcision for Gentile believers and carried the question to Jerusalem, where the apostles and elders agreed with them (Acts 15:1–29). Paul then split from Barnabas over John Mark and set out with Silas (Acts 15:36–41). At Lystra he took on Timothy and circumcised him because of the local Jews (Acts 16:1–3), a step that has long puzzled readers of Galatians. Guided by the Spirit and a vision, he crossed to Macedonia: at Philippi he was beaten and jailed, then used his Roman citizenship to demand a public release (Acts 16:11–40); at Thessalonica and Berea he argued from the Scriptures in the synagogues and was driven out by opponents (Acts 17:1–15); in Athens he debated with philosophers and spoke before the Areopagus (Acts 17:16–34). His letters to the Philippians and Thessalonians were written to churches founded on this journey.
sections.refs: Acts 15:1–41; Acts 16:1–40; Acts 17:1–34; Galatians 2:1–10; Philippians 1:3–8; 1 Thessalonians 1:5–10; 1 Thessalonians 2:1–2
